Adult Scaled herring (Harengula jaguana) in the Gulf of Mexico attain a maximum total length of 21.2 cm [Li = 21.2 cm], placing them among the larger members of the genus. This ultimate size is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 101.2 grams [Wwi = 101.2 grams], which represents the heaviest individuals recorded during extensive field sampling. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical clupeid allometric curve, with length accounting for most of the variation in weight among mature specimens. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Harengula clupeola reveal that H. jaguana attains a somewhat larger asymptotic size, a difference that may be linked to its exploitation of more productive coastal nursery habitats. The maximum body mass of 101.2 grams [Wwi = 101.2 grams] is achieved only by the oldest and most robust individuals, which are usually found in offshore aggregations where prey availability remains consistently high throughout the year.

Reproductive development in Scaled herring proceeds in synchrony with body size, and the onset of puberty occurs when individuals reach a total length of 8.1 cm [Lp = 8.1 cm]. At this developmental milestone, the average wet weight at puberty is 5.38 grams [Wwp = 5.38 grams], reflecting a tenfold increase from the mass at birth. This length-based threshold for maturation is comparable to values reported for other tropical clupeids, where a minimum body size serves as a proximate cue for gonadal activation. Individuals that have not yet attained 8.1 cm [Lp = 8.1 cm] in total length remain reproductively inactive, directing all available resources toward somatic growth. The relationship between length and maturation is robust across populations, although slight variation exists depending on local thermal regimes and food supply, with faster-growing fish reaching the puberty threshold earlier in the season.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], the embryonic development of Harengula jaguana culminates in hatching after an incubation period of just 6 days [ab = 6 days]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a wet weight at birth of 0.0024 grams [Wwb = 0.0024 grams], a remarkably small starting mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves typical of pelagic-spawning clupeids. This neonatal mass is derived from the egg diameter of 1.66 mm, which yields a spherical volume and translates into minimal maternal investment per offspring. The rapid hatching at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C] is advantageous in warm coastal waters where predation pressure on vulnerable early life stages is intense, and it allows the prolarvae to quickly begin exogenous feeding. Temperature-dependence of the hatching interval is pronounced, with cooler conditions prolonging the yolk-sac stage considerably.

The maximum reproductive output of Scaled herring has been quantified under optimal thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], females produce a clutch of approximately 7,250 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 7,250 eggs per spawning event], with a spawning frequency of one event every 51 days [F_R_i = one event every 51 days]. This high fecundity per event is among the highest recorded for any clupeid of comparable body size, reflecting the species' life-history strategy of high fecundity and low maternal investment per offspring. The reproductive season extends over several months, allowing multiple spawning events to accumulate substantial lifetime fecundity. The warm thermal regime at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C] accelerates vitellogenesis and gonad recrudescence, enabling the rapid turnover of successive batches.

Longevity records for Harengula jaguana indicate a maximum lifespan of 3 years [am = 3 years] when maintained under continuous thermal conditions of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. This relatively short life span is typical of small, fast-growing tropical clupeids that mature quickly and invest heavily in early reproduction. The oldest individuals collected during field surveys in the Gulf of Mexico reached an age of about 1095 days [am = about 1095 days], consistent with the captive data and confirming that senescence begins shortly after the second reproductive season at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. The ultimate total length of 21.2 cm [Li = 21.2 cm] is attained within the first two years, after which growth slows considerably as resources are diverted toward gamete production. This compressed life history, combining rapid juvenile growth, early maturation at 8.1 cm [Lp = 8.1 cm], and a short reproductive window, reflects an adaptation to the variable and often unpredictable conditions of nearshore environments where Harengula jaguana is most abundant.
